title: ARTICLE ARCHIVE Education Don't Ditch That Textbook
author: Sol in the Wild
summary: The author pushes back against the Ditch That Textbook movement, arguing its alternatives -- gamified lessons, digital scavenger hunts, AI-generated activities -- prioritise the appearance of engagement over actual learning. Drawing on cognitive science, the essay argues that simple, well-structured instructional practices (clear explanation, retrieval, writing, discussion, feedback) align with how learning actually happens and are cognitively superior to overdesigned novelty. Students can detect performative engagement: they know when adults are trying too hard, and lessons designed to mimic TikTok feel less authentic than quiet intellectual grappling. Excessive decorative complexity in lesson design competes for the limited working memory that should be focused on the content itself. The author does not argue for nostalgia but for clarity: simple practices are not simple because they are traditional but because they work. The revolution education needs is not increasingly elaborate disguises for learning but a rediscovery of the power of simply teaching well.
points: - Students detect performative engagement: they know when adults are trying too hard, and lessons designed to mimic TikTok feel less authentic to students than quiet intellectual grappling with real ideas. - Overdesigned instruction creates unnecessary cognitive load -- every decorative slide, multi-app workflow, and fun layer competes for the limited working memory that should be processing the content itself. - Simple classroom practices (teacher explanation, writing, retrieval, discussion) are not merely traditional -- they are cognitively superior because they match how knowledge is actually built and consolidated over time. - The confusion in education between complexity and rigour, and between entertainment and engagement, has led teachers to dress up learning in gimmicks that undermine the very thing they intend to support. - The revision education needs is not a new technology or engagement strategy but a return to the principle that the most powerful classroom practices -- though they look ordinary -- are the ones that reliably produce learning.
quotes: For years, education has been flooded with messages telling teachers to move beyond traditional instruction. Ditch the textbook. Ditch lectures. Ditch worksheets. Ditch rote practice. Ditch pencil-and-paper tasks.

Students can tell the difference between authentic intellectual work and performative engagement. One feels real. The other feels forced. Students are incredibly good at detecting when adults are trying too hard.

In fact, overdesigned instruction often creates unnecessary distractions. Every decorative slide, complicated procedure, multiple-app workflow, or fun layer students must navigate competes for limited attention and working memory. Instead of supporting thinking, it can overload it.

Simple is not simplistic. Simple is often cognitively superior. A coherent reading. A well-structured explanation. Repeated practice. Writing. Thinking. Retrieval. Discussion. Reflection. Feedback. These processes work because they align with how learning actually happens.

There is something deeply authentic about classrooms centered on thinking rather than performance. A room where students are actively wrestling with knowledge instead of constantly consuming polished activities designed to keep them superficially entertained.

Not every lesson needs to feel like a game show. Not every activity needs to mimic TikTok. Not every classroom task needs a gimmick attached to it to justify its existence. More often than not, students simply need to quietly grapple with important ideas.

They aren't ordinary because they are nostalgic or traditional. But because they work. The revolution we need in education is not finding increasingly elaborate ways to disguise learning. It is rediscovering the power of simply teaching well.
